"Jupiter," he said when we reached the foot of the tree, "come here. Was the skull nailed to the branch with its face turned outward, or with its face toward the branch?"

"The face was out, master, so the crows could get at the eyes easily, without any trouble."

"Well then, was it through this eye or that one that you dropped the beetle?" As he spoke, Legrand touched each of Jupiter's eyes.

"It was this eye, master, the left eye, just as you told me," and as he said it, the man pointed to his right eye.

"That will do. We must try again."

My friend, whose madness now seemed to me, or at least I imagined it seemed, to have some signs of method in it, moved the peg that marked where the beetle had fallen. He placed it about three inches west of its first position. Then he took the tape measure again from the nearest point of the tree trunk to the peg, as before, and carried the line straight onward for fifty feet. This marked a new spot, several yards away from the place where we had been digging.

Around this new spot he drew a circle, a little larger than the first, and we began again with our spades. I was terribly tired, yet I no longer felt much dislike for the work, though I hardly understood what had changed my feelings. I had become strangely interested, even excited. Perhaps there was something in Legrand's wild behavior, some sense of planning or careful thought, that affected me. I dug eagerly, and from time to time I caught myself actually looking with something very like expectation for the imaginary treasure whose vision had driven my poor companion out of his senses. While these wandering thoughts held me most strongly, and after we had worked perhaps an hour and a half, we were interrupted again by the dog's violent howling. At first his restlessness had clearly been only play or whim, but now his tone was bitter and serious. When Jupiter again tried to muzzle him, the dog resisted fiercely, jumped into the hole, and tore at the earth madly with his claws. In a few seconds he had uncovered a mass of human bones, making two complete skeletons, mixed with several metal buttons and what seemed to be dust from decayed woolen cloth. One or two strokes of a spade turned up the blade of a large Spanish knife, and as we dug farther, three or four loose gold and silver coins came into view.

The night was dark and stormy. Not a single star trembled in the sky above, while the deep roll of heavy thunder kept shaking in the ear. Terrible lightning flashed angrily through the clouded chambers of heaven, seeming to mock the power that the famous Franklin had claimed over its terror. Even the rough winds came out together from their mysterious homes and roared about, as if they meant to make the wild scene wilder still.

At such a time, so dark and gloomy, my whole spirit longed for human sympathy; but instead of that,

'My dearest friend, my counsellor, my comforter and guide, my joy in grief, my second happiness in joy,' came to my side.

Her step was so soft that it made no sound, and if her kind touch had not sent a magical thrill through me, she might have slipped away unnoticed and uncalled, like other quiet beauties. A strange sadness lay on her face, like frozen tears on December's robe, as she pointed to the struggling elements outside and told me to consider the two beings shown there.

In his hope of conquering Constantinople, he looked toward an event that would stand like a marker in the empty stretch of ages, an achievement unmatched in human history. That famous city, whose setting was admired by the whole world, and which for many centuries had been a stronghold of the Moslems, would be rescued from slavery and barbarism and returned to a people known for genius, civilization, and love of liberty. Perdita rested in his restored company, in his love, his hopes, and his fame, as if lying on a rich couch; every thought was joy, and every feeling seemed bathed in a warm and friendly air.

We reached Kishan on the seventh of July. The weather during our journey had been clear and calm. Each day, before dawn, we left our night's camp and watched the shadows draw back from hills and valleys before the golden brightness of the rising sun. The soldiers with us, with their national liveliness, took enthusiastic pleasure in the beauty of nature. The rising of the sun was greeted with triumphant music, while the birds, heard in scattered bursts, filled the pauses between the notes. At noon we pitched our tents in some shaded valley or wooded shelter among the mountains, while a stream murmuring over stones brought grateful sleep. Our evening march, calmer than the restless morning, was even more delightful. If the band played, they seemed without planning it to choose gentler tunes: a lover's farewell, or a lament for absence, would be followed and ended by some solemn hymn that suited the peaceful beauty of evening and lifted the mind toward grand and religious thoughts. Often every sound stopped so that we could listen to the nightingale, while fireflies danced in bright patterns and the soft cry of the aziolo promised fair weather to the travelers. When we passed through a valley, soft shadows surrounded us and rocks glowed with beautiful colors. When we crossed a mountain, Greece spread below like a living map, her famous peaks cutting the sky and her rivers drawing silver lines through the fertile land. Almost afraid to breathe, we English travelers looked in delight at this splendid landscape, so different from the quiet colors and sad graces of our own country. When we left Macedonia, the fertile but low plains of Thrace offered fewer beauties, yet the journey remained interesting. An advance guard announced our approach, and the country people quickly stirred themselves to honor Lord Raymond.

"Now notice what it means to leave the pure ways that He loves, and to play with worldly things that offend Him. These monks went into the bath and came out washed as white as snow; and behold, at that very moment His sign appeared in a miraculous rebuke. His insulted waters stopped flowing and vanished completely."

"They got off lightly, Sandy, considering how that sort of crime is treated in this country."

"Perhaps; but it was their first sin. They had lived perfectly for a long time, and differed in nothing from angels. Prayers, tears, and tortures of the flesh were all useless in persuading the water to flow again. Even processions, even burnt offerings, even candles promised to the Virgin, all failed, every one of them, and the whole land wondered."

"How odd to find that even this business has its financial panics, and sometimes sees its paper money and greenbacks sink to nothing, until everything stops. Go on, Sandy."

"And so, after a year and a day, the good abbot humbly surrendered and destroyed the bath. And behold, His anger was at that moment satisfied, and the waters poured out richly again, and to this very day they have never stopped flowing in that generous amount."

"Then I suppose nobody has washed since."

"Anyone who tried it could have a noose for nothing; yes, and he would need it quickly too."

"The community has prospered since then?"

"From that very day. The fame of the miracle spread abroad into every land. Monks came from everywhere to join; they came like fish, in schools. The monastery added building to building, and then others to those, and so it spread its arms wide and took them in. Nuns came also; then more, and more again. They built across from the monastery on the other side of the valley and added building to building until the nunnery became mighty. The monks and nuns were friendly with one another, and they joined their loving labors together, and together they built a fine great foundling asylum halfway down the valley between them."

"You spoke of some hermits, Sandy."

"They have gathered there from the ends of the earth. A hermit does best where there are crowds of pilgrims. You will find no kind of hermit missing. If anyone mentions a kind of hermit he thinks is new and only found in some distant strange land, let him merely search among the holes and caves and swamps that line that Valley of Holiness, and whatever his type may be, it does not matter; he will find a sample of it there."

If I avoid claiming property so valuable, property that I am known to possess, I will at least make the animal suspicious. It is not wise for me to draw attention either to myself or to the beast. At that moment we heard a step on the stairs.

"Be ready," said Dupin, "with your pistols, but do not use them or show them until I give the signal."

The front door of the house had been left open, and the visitor had entered without ringing and had already climbed several steps. Now, however, he seemed to hesitate. Soon we heard him going down again. Dupin was moving quickly toward the door when we heard him coming up once more. He did not turn back a second time, but came up firmly and knocked at the door of our room.

"Come in," said Dupin, in a cheerful, hearty voice.

A man entered. He was plainly a sailor, tall, strong, and muscular, with a reckless expression on his face that was not entirely unpleasant.

He said he was wasting his time where he was, and that letters from the friends he had made in London urged him to return and complete the negotiations they had begun for his Indian enterprise. He could no longer delay his departure. But since his journey to London might be followed, perhaps sooner than he now guessed, by his longer voyage, he begged me to give him as much of my company as I could spare. He therefore asked me to leave my lonely island and meet him at Perth, so that we might travel south together. This letter partly brought me back to life, and I decided to leave my island after two days had passed.

Yet before I left, there was a task to be done, and I shuddered to think of it. I had to pack up my chemical instruments, and for that purpose I had to enter the room that had been the scene of my hateful work. I had to touch the tools whose very sight made me sick. The next morning at daybreak I gathered enough courage and unlocked the door of my laboratory. The remains of the half-finished creature I had destroyed lay scattered on the floor, and I almost felt as if I had torn apart the living flesh of a human being. I paused to steady myself and then entered the room. With a trembling hand I carried the instruments out; but I realized that I should not leave the relics of my work where they might fill the peasants with horror and suspicion. So I put them into a basket with a large number of stones, laid them aside, and decided to throw them into the sea that very night. Meanwhile I sat on the beach, cleaning and arranging my chemical apparatus.

Nothing could have been more complete than the change in my feelings since the night when the demon appeared. Before then I had looked on my promise with dark despair as something that had to be fulfilled, whatever the consequences might be. Now I felt as if a film had been removed from my eyes and I was seeing clearly for the first time. The thought of beginning my labors again did not enter my mind for a single instant. The threat I had heard weighed heavily on my thoughts, but I did not consider that any voluntary act of mine could prevent it. I had resolved that to create another being like the fiend I first made would be the lowest and most terrible selfishness. I drove from my mind every thought that could lead me to any other conclusion.

I rose early in the morning and again managed to escape the watchfulness of my creditors. I hurried to the bookseller's stall and spent the little cash I had on several books about mechanics and practical astronomy. When I reached home safely with them, I gave every spare moment to reading them, and soon made enough progress in those studies, as I thought, to carry out my plan. During this time I made every effort to soften the feelings of the three creditors who had troubled me so much. At last I succeeded, partly by selling enough of my household furniture to pay half of what I owed them, and partly by promising to pay the rest when I completed a small project I said I had in mind. I also asked for their help with it. By these means, since they were ignorant men, I found little difficulty in winning them over to my purpose.

"Once these matters had been arranged in a friendly way, I managed, with my wife's help and with the greatest secrecy and care, to sell what property I still had and to borrow small sums under various excuses. I gave no thought to how I would repay the money later, but in this way I collected a considerable amount of ready cash. With these funds I bought, at different times, very fine cambric muslin in pieces of twelve yards each; twine; a quantity of caoutchouc varnish; a large, deep wicker basket made to order; and several other items needed to build and equip a balloon of extraordinary size. I instructed my wife to make it up as quickly as possible and gave her all the necessary details about the method. Meanwhile I worked the twine into a net of sufficient size, fitted it with a hoop and the required cords, and bought a quadrant, a compass, a spyglass, a common barometer with some important changes, and two astronomical instruments not generally known. I then took chances at night to carry, to a lonely place east of Rotterdam, five iron-bound casks holding about fifty gallons each, one larger cask, six tin tubes three inches across, properly shaped and ten feet long, a quantity of a particular metal or half-metal that I will not name, and a dozen large bottles of a common acid. The gas made from these last materials is a gas no one else has ever produced, or at least never used for any similar purpose. I would not hesitate to reveal the secret, except that it rightfully belongs to a citizen of Nantz, in France, who shared it with me under conditions."

The doctor was an old man, and a very nice, kind-looking old man when I got him awake. I told him that my brother and I had been over on Spanish Island hunting the afternoon before, and that we had camped on a piece of raft we found. About midnight, I said, my brother must have kicked his gun in his sleep, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted the doctor to go over there and fix it, and not say anything or let anyone know, because we meant to come home that evening and surprise the family.

"Who are your people?" he says.

"The Phelpses, down yonder."

"Oh," he says. Then after a minute he says:

"How did you say he got shot?"

"He had a dream," I says, "and it shot him."

"A strange dream," he says.

So he lit his lantern, got his saddle-bags, and we started. But when he saw the canoe, he did not like the look of it. He said it was big enough for one person, but did not look very safe for two. I says:

"Oh, you needn't be afraid, sir. She carried the three of us easily enough."

"What three?"

"Why, me and Sid, and-and-and the guns; that's what I mean."

"Oh," he says.

But he put his foot on the gunwale and rocked the canoe, then shook his head and said he guessed he would look around for a bigger one. But all the others were locked and chained, so he took my canoe and told me to wait until he came back. Or, he said, I could look around some more, or maybe I had better go home and get them ready for the surprise, if I wanted to. I said I did not, so I told him exactly how to find the raft, and then he set off.

Pretty soon an idea struck me. I says to myself, suppose he cannot fix that leg in three shakes of a sheep's tail, as the saying is? Suppose it takes him three or four days? What are we going to do, lie around there until he lets the secret out? No, sir; I know what I will do. I will wait, and when he comes back, if he says he has to go again, I will get down there too, even if I have to swim. Then we will tie him up and keep him with us, and push off down the river; and when Tom is done with him, we will pay him what it is worth, or all we have, and then let him get ashore.

So then I crawled into a lumber pile to get some sleep. The next time I woke, the sun was high over my head. I jumped out and went to the doctor's house, but they told me he had gone away sometime in the night and had not come back yet.

'Oh, never mind my hat! I want Virginia!' cried the little Duke, laughing, and they galloped on to the railway station. There Mr. Otis asked the station-master whether anyone matching Virginia's description had been seen on the platform, but he could learn nothing about her. The station-master, however, sent messages up and down the line and assured him that a careful watch would be kept. After buying a hat for the little Duke from a linen-draper who was just closing his shop, Mr. Otis rode off to Bexley, a village about four miles away. He had been told that gypsies often stayed there, because there was a large common beside it. There they woke the country policeman, but got no information from him, and after riding all over the common they turned their horses toward home. They reached the Chase about eleven o'clock, completely tired out and almost heart-broken. They found Washington and the twins waiting at the gate-house with lanterns, because the avenue was very dark. Not the slightest trace of Virginia had been found. The gypsies had been caught on Brockley meadows, but she was not with them. They had explained their sudden departure by saying they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and had left in a hurry for fear of arriving late. In fact, they had been quite upset to hear that Virginia was missing, since they were grateful to Mr. Otis for allowing them to camp in his park, and four of them had stayed behind to help search. The carp-pond had been dragged, and the whole Chase had been searched thoroughly, but nothing had come of it. It was clear that, for that night at least, Virginia was lost to them. In the deepest sadness Mr. Otis and the boys walked up to the house, with the groom following behind with the two horses and the pony. In the hall they found a group of frightened servants, and poor Mrs. Otis was lying on a sofa in the library, almost out of her mind with fear and anxiety, while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with eau-de-cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted that she eat something and ordered supper for everyone. It was a gloomy meal, for hardly anyone spoke. Even the twins were awed and quiet, since they were very fond of their sister. When they had finished, Mr. Otis, despite the little Duke's pleas, ordered them all to bed, saying that nothing more could be done that night and that in the morning he would telegraph Scotland Yard to send detectives at once.

"They had better not!" said Mr. Bumble, clenching his fist. "Let me see any man, parish or outside parish, who would presume to do it, and I can tell him he would not do it a second time!"

Without any violent gestures, this might not have seemed a very high compliment to the lady's charms. But because Mr. Bumble made the threat with many warlike movements, she was deeply touched by this proof of his devotion and declared, with great admiration, that he was truly a dove.

The dove then turned up his coat collar and put on his cocked hat. After exchanging a long and loving embrace with his future partner, he once again faced the cold night wind. He paused only a few minutes in the male paupers' ward to abuse them a little, in order to satisfy himself that he could fill the office of workhouse-master with the necessary sharpness. Certain of his qualifications, Mr. Bumble left the building with a light heart and bright visions of his future promotion, which occupied his mind until he reached the undertaker's shop.

Other chances to make her observations were sure to come. Anne had soon been in company with all four of them often enough to form an opinion, though she was too wise to admit it at home, where she knew it would satisfy neither husband nor wife. She thought Louisa was rather the favorite, yet, as far as she dared judge from memory and experience, she could not believe that Captain Wentworth was in love with either young woman. They were more in love with him; and yet even there it was not truly love. It was a small fever of admiration, though it might, and probably must, end in love for some of them. Charles Hayter seemed aware that he was being slighted, and Henrietta sometimes appeared divided between the two men. Anne longed for the power to show them all what they were doing and to point out some of the troubles they were exposing themselves to. She blamed no one for deceit. It was a great comfort to her to believe Captain Wentworth was not at all aware of the pain he was causing. There was no triumph, no shabby triumph, in his manner. He had probably never heard of Charles Hayter's claims and had never thought of them. His only fault was accepting the attentions, for accepting must be the word, of two young women at the same time.

After a short struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to leave the field. Three days passed without his coming once to Uppercross, a very clear change. He had even refused one regular dinner invitation. When Mr. Musgrove found him with several large books before him, Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove became sure that all was not right and spoke with serious faces of his studying himself to death. Mary hoped and believed that Henrietta had positively dismissed him, while her husband constantly expected to see him tomorrow. Anne could only feel that Charles Hayter was wise.

One morning around this time, while Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth had gone shooting together, the sisters in the Cottage were sitting quietly at work. They were then visited at the window by the sisters from the Mansion-house.

It was a very fine November day, and the Miss Musgroves came through the little grounds and stopped for no other reason than to say they were going to take a long walk. They therefore assumed Mary would not like to go with them. When Mary immediately replied, with some jealousy at not being considered a good walker, "Oh, yes, I should like to join you very much; I am very fond of a long walk," Anne felt certain, from the looks of the two girls, that this was exactly what they did not want. She again admired the sort of necessity that family habits seemed to create, by which everything had to be communicated and everything had to be done together, however unwanted and inconvenient it might be.

'Well, monsieur le mauvais sujet,' cried the old lady as he came into the room, 'why have you not been to see me all this time?'

'My dear Lady Clem, I never have a moment to myself,' said Lord Arthur, smiling.

'I suppose you mean you spend all day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying chiffons and talking nonsense. I cannot understand why people make such a fuss about getting married. In my day we never dreamed of billing and cooing in public, or in private either, for that matter.'

'I assure you I have not seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she belongs entirely to her dressmakers.'

'Of course. That is the only reason you come to see an ugly old woman like me. I wonder you men do not take warning. On a fait des folies pour moi, and here I am now, a poor rheumatic creature with false hair and a bad temper. Why, if dear Lady Jansen did not send me all the worst French novels she can find, I do not think I could get through the day. Doctors are no use at all except to take fees from one. They cannot even cure my heartburn.'

'I have brought you a cure for that, Lady Clem,' said Lord Arthur gravely. 'It is a wonderful thing, invented by an American.'

'I do not think I like American inventions, Arthur. I am quite sure I do not. I read some American novels lately, and they were complete nonsense.'

'Oh, but there is no nonsense at all about this, Lady Clem. I assure you it is a perfect cure. You must promise to try it.' Lord Arthur took the little box from his pocket and handed it to her.

'Well, the box is charming, Arthur. Is it really a present? That is very sweet of you. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks like a bonbon. I will take it at once.'

'Good heavens, Lady Clem!' cried Lord Arthur, catching her hand. 'You must not do anything of the kind. It is a homeopathic medicine, and if you take it when you do not have heartburn, it might do you a great deal of harm. Wait until you have an attack, and take it then. You will be astonished by the result.'

'I should like to take it now,' said Lady Clementina, holding the little transparent capsule up to the light, with its floating bubble of liquid aconitine. 'I am sure it is delicious. The fact is that, though I hate doctors, I love medicines. However, I will keep it until my next attack.'

'And when will that be?' asked Lord Arthur eagerly.

He seemed to deliberately misunderstand the word she had repeated, and added hurriedly, "Yes, customers; in banking we usually call our connections our customers. He was a French gentleman, a scientific gentleman, a man of great learning, a doctor."

"Not from Beauvais?"

"Why, yes, from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman was from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, he was well known in Paris. I had the honor of knowing him there. Our relations were business relations, but confidential ones. I was then in our French House, and had been there, oh, twenty years."

"At that time, may I ask what time, sir?"

"I speak, miss, of twenty years ago. He married an English lady, and I was one of the trustees. His affairs, like the affairs of many other French gentlemen and French families, were entirely in Tellson's hands. In the same way, I am, or have been, trustee of one kind or another for scores of our customers. These are only business relations, miss; there is no friendship in them, no special interest, nothing like sentiment. I have passed from one to another during my business life just as I pass from one customer to another during my business day. In short, I have no feelings. I am a mere machine. To continue-"

"But this is my father's story, sir; and I begin to think"-her strangely tightened forehead was fixed very closely on him-"that when I was left an orphan, because my mother survived my father by only two years, it was you who brought me to England. I am almost sure it was you."

Mr. Lorry took the small hesitant hand that trustingly reached for his and raised it with some ceremony to his lips. He then led the young lady straight back to her chair, and, holding the back of it with his left hand, used his right hand in turn to rub his chin, pull his wig at the ears, or emphasize what he said. He stood looking down into her face while she sat looking up into his.

"Miss Manette, it was I. And you will see how truly I spoke of myself just now, when I said I had no feelings and that all my relations with my fellow creatures are only business relations, when you remember that I have never seen you since. No; you have been the ward of Tellson's House since then, and I have been busy with the other business of Tellson's House since then. Feelings! I have no time for them, no chance for them. I spend my whole life, miss, turning an immense money mangle."

"She and the children might stay very well."

"Ah, papa, that is what you have never been able to manage, and I do not think you ever will. Isabella cannot bear to stay behind her husband."

This was too true to deny. Though it was unwelcome, Mr. Woodhouse could only sigh submissively. When Emma saw that his spirits were lowered by the thought of his daughter's attachment to her husband, she immediately turned to a part of the subject that would cheer him.

"Harriet must give us as much of her company as she can while my brother and sister are here. I am sure she will be pleased with the children. We are very proud of the children, are we not, papa? I wonder which one she will think handsomer, Henry or John?"

"Yes, I wonder which she will. Poor little dears, how glad they will be to come. They are very fond of being at Hartfield, Harriet."

"I dare say they are, sir. I am sure I do not know anyone who is not."

"Henry is a fine boy, but John is very like his mama. Henry is the eldest; he was named after me, not after his father. John, the second, is named after his father. Some people are surprised, I believe, that the eldest was not named for him, but Isabella would have him called Henry, which I thought very pretty of her. And he is a very clever boy indeed. They are all remarkably clever, and they have so many pretty ways. They will come and stand by my chair and say, 'Grandpapa, can you give me a bit of string?' Once Henry asked me for a knife, but I told him knives were only made for grandpapas. I think their father is often too rough with them."

"He seems rough to you," said Emma, "because you are so very gentle yourself. But if you could compare him with other fathers, you would not think him rough. He wants his boys to be active and hardy, and if they behave badly, he can give them a sharp word now and then. But he is an affectionate father; certainly Mr. John Knightley is an affectionate father. The children are all fond of him."

"And then their uncle comes in and tosses them up to the ceiling in a very frightening way!"

"But they like it, papa. There is nothing they like so much. It gives them such enjoyment that, if their uncle did not make the rule that they must take turns, whichever one began would never give way to the other."

"Well, I cannot understand it."

"That is true of us all, papa. One half of the world cannot understand the pleasures of the other."

Was my love blameworthy? If it was, I did not know it. I desired only what I already possessed, and if your looks, your words, and your innocent caresses gave me a delight usually kept apart from a parent's feelings toward a child, still no uneasiness, no wish, no passing thought woke me to any sense of guilt. I loved you as a human father might be imagined to love a daughter born to him by a heavenly mother; as Anchises might have looked on the child of Venus if the child had been a daughter. My love was mixed with respect and worship. Perhaps, too, my passion was lulled into contentment by the deep and exclusive affection you felt for me.

"But when I saw you become the object of another person's love; when I imagined that you might be loved in some way other than as a sacred image of beauty and goodness, or that you might love another with a warmer affection than the one you gave me, then the fiend inside me awoke. I sent your lover away, and from that moment I have known no peace. I have searched in vain for sleep and rest; my eyelids refused to close, and my blood was forever in turmoil. I woke to a new life, like someone who dies in hope and wakes in Hell. I will not soil your imagination by describing my battles, my anger at myself, and my despair. Let a veil be drawn over the unimaginable feelings of a guilty father; the secrets of a heart in such agony must not be made common. All was confusion, crime, remorse, and hate, yet still the most tender love remained. What first woke in me the firm resolve to conquer my passion and restore her father to my child was the sight of your bitter and sympathetic sorrows. That was what led me here. I thought that if I could awaken again in my heart the grief I had felt at losing your mother, and all the memories of her that had slept for seventeen years, then all love for her child would die out. In a fit of heroism I decided to go alone, to leave you, the life of my life, and not see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it would not work. I judged my strength too high, or my love too low. I would certainly have died if you had not hurried to me. Would that I had indeed been extinguished!

"And now, Mathilda, I must make my last confession. I have been miserably wrong in imagining that I could conquer my love for you. I never can.

"Good-bye, Uncle George. I shall be late for lunch if I stay any longer. Thank you for giving me the information I wanted. I always like to know everything about my new friends and nothing about my old ones."

"Where are you lunching, Harry?"

"At Aunt Agatha's. I have invited myself and Mr. Gray. He is her latest protege."

"Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, not to trouble me any more with her charity appeals. I am tired of them. Why, the good woman seems to think I have nothing to do but write cheques for her foolish schemes."

"All right, Uncle George, I will tell her, but it will have no effect. Philanthropic people lose all sense of humanity. That is their special mark."

The old gentleman growled in approval and rang the bell for his servant. Lord Henry passed under the low arcade into Burlington Street and turned toward Berkeley Square.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray's parentage. Roughly as it had been told to him, it had still stirred him by suggesting a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a mad passion. A few wild weeks of happiness ended by a horrible, treacherous crime. Months of silent agony, and then a child born in pain. The mother snatched away by death, the boy left to loneliness and to the rule of an old, loveless man. Yes, it was an interesting background. It gave the lad a setting and made him seem more perfect. Behind every exquisite thing that existed, there was something tragic. Worlds had to suffer birth pains for even the smallest flower to bloom. And how charming he had been at dinner the night before, sitting opposite him at the club with startled eyes and parted lips, frightened and pleased, while the red candle-shades deepened the rosy wonder waking in his face. Talking to him was like playing on an exquisite violin. He responded to every touch and every thrill of the bow. There was something terribly fascinating in the use of influence. No other activity was like it. To project one's soul into some graceful form and let it remain there for a moment; to hear one's own ideas echoed back with all the added music of passion and youth; to pass one's temperament into another as if it were a delicate liquid or a strange perfume, there was real joy in that, perhaps the most satisfying joy left to us in an age so limited and vulgar as ours, an age coarse in its pleasures and common in its aims. He was a marvelous type too, this boy whom chance had brought him in Basil's studio, or at least he could be shaped into a marvelous type.

The day passed much as the day before had passed. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent several hours of the morning with the invalid, who continued to improve, though slowly. In the evening Elizabeth joined their party in the drawing-room. The loo table, however, did not appear. Mr. Darcy was writing, and Miss Bingley, sitting near him, watched the progress of his letter and repeatedly drew his attention away by sending messages to his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, and Mrs. Hurst was watching their game.

Elizabeth took up some needlework and found enough amusement in listening to what passed between Darcy and his companion. The lady's constant praises of his handwriting, the evenness of his lines, and the length of his letter, together with the perfect indifference with which he received her compliments, made a curious conversation and suited exactly Elizabeth's opinion of them both.

"How delighted Miss Darcy will be to receive such a letter!"

He made no answer.

"You write unusually fast."

"You are mistaken. I write rather slowly."

"How many letters you must have to write in a year! Business letters too! How hateful I should find them!"

"It is fortunate, then, that they fall to me instead of to you."

"Please tell your sister that I long to see her."

"I have already told her so once, at your request."

"I am afraid you do not like your pen. Let me mend it for you. I mend pens remarkably well."

"Thank you, but I always mend my own."

"How do you manage to write so evenly?"

He was silent.

"Tell your sister I am delighted to hear of her improvement on the harp, and please let her know that I am quite enchanted with her beautiful little design for a table. I think it infinitely better than Miss Grantley's."

"Will you allow me to save your raptures until I write again? At present I have not enough room to do them justice."

"Oh, it is of no importance. I shall see her in January. But do you always write such charming long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?"

"They are generally long; but whether they are always charming is not for me to decide."

"It is a rule with me that a person who can write a long letter easily cannot write badly."

"That will not do as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline," cried her brother, "because he does not write easily. He studies too much for words of four syllables. Do you not, Darcy?"

"My style of writing is very different from yours."

"Oh," cried Miss Bingley, "Charles writes in the most careless way imaginable."

"Unless you call Miss Havisham a he. And I doubt even you will go that far."

"Miss Havisham, up town?" said Joe.

"Is there any Miss Havisham down town?" my sister returned.

"She wants this boy to go and play there. And of course he is going. And he had better play there," said my sister, shaking her head at me as if encouraging me to be especially cheerful and playful, "or I will work him."

I had heard of Miss Havisham up town. Everyone for miles around had heard of Miss Havisham up town, as an immensely rich and grim lady who lived in a large, gloomy house barricaded against robbers and lived a shut-away life.

"Well, to be sure!" said Joe, astonished. "I wonder how she came to know Pip!"

"Noodle!" cried my sister. "Who said she knew him?"

"Which some individual," Joe politely suggested again, "mentioned that she wanted him to go and play there."

"And couldn't she ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go and play there? Is it not just barely possible that Uncle Pumblechook may be a tenant of hers, and that he may sometimes, we will not say quarterly or half-yearly, for that would be expecting too much of you, but sometimes go there to pay his rent? And couldn't she then ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go and play there? And couldn't Uncle Pumblechook, being always considerate and thoughtful toward us, though you may not think so, Joseph," she said in a tone of deep reproach, as if he were the hardest-hearted of nephews, "then mention this boy, standing prancing here," which I solemnly declare I was not doing, "that I have forever been a willing slave to?"

"Good again!" cried Uncle Pumblechook. "Well put! Nicely pointed! Good indeed! Now, Joseph, you know the case."

"No, Joseph," said my sister, still reproachfully, while Joe apologetically rubbed the back of his hand across his nose again and again, "you do not yet, though you may not think so, know the case. You may believe you do, but you do not, Joseph. For you do not know that Uncle Pumblechook, realizing that for all we can tell this boy's fortune may be made by going to Miss Havisham's, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, keep him tonight, and take him with his own hands to Miss Havisham's tomorrow morning. And Lord have mercy on me!" cried my sister, suddenly tearing off her bonnet in desperation, "here I stand talking to mere mooncalves, with Uncle Pumblechook waiting, the mare catching cold at the door, and the boy blackened with soot and dirt from the hair of his head to the sole of his foot!"
